symptom: Airbag lamp, unused passenger bag, or a 2001–2015 Honda/Acura you are about to buy
years: 2001–2016 (verify VIN — 2003 Accord is in the population)
pattern: Takata ammonium-nitrate inflators can rupture when they deploy. Metal fragments enter the cabin. Age, heat, and humidity make unused passenger inflators worse, not better. A 2003 Honda Accord is the bay’s demo car for a reason: run that VIN on SaferCar before you shop a used module or ignore an SRS lamp.
notATsb: This is a public NHTSA recall / campaign pointer, not a dealer TSB PDF and not a copied ALLDATA bulletin. We do not paste inflator part lists.
dummyMove: Identify the VIN on /recalls and at nhtsa.gov/recalls. If SaferCar says the inflator is open, that is a dealer campaign — not an indie “we can get a bag from the yard.”
geniusNote: An unused passenger inflator can sit for 15–20 years and then fail on the first real hit. The recall is the inflator (and often the module it lives in), not “the whole dash is junk.” Do not buy a used airbag. The campaign exists because salvage bags are how this repeats.

symptom: SRS lamp or a used car from the mid-2000s through mid-2010s
pattern: Takata inflators were used across dozens of brands. The official campaign page lists affected automakers. A clean Carfax does not close an open inflator. A yard module is how people re-install the defect.
notATsb: Public NHTSA campaign page. We will not reproduce OEM TSB text or inflator serial tables.
dummyMove: Type the 17-character VIN at SaferCar. If the car is in the bay, use /recalls. Do not shop Facebook airbags.
geniusNote: Driver and passenger inflators are different campaigns on many VINs. One closed recall does not mean the other side is done. Read both lines.

symptom: Check-engine lamp, P0420 or P0430, no obvious misfire
pattern: Catalyst efficiency below threshold. Shops jump to a converter. Public complaint files and every honest tech bay start with exhaust leaks before the rear O2, a lazy sensor, and misfire history that already melted the brick.
notATsb: A generic OBD pattern, not a stolen brand TSB. Ask the shop if they have an OEM bulletin — have them show the number and the measurement. We will not paste the PDF.
dummyMove: Translate the code on /obd. Ask for freeze-frame (ECT, mph, load) and a leak check before anyone prices stainless.
geniusNote: If STFT/LTFT were wild or a misfire counter was high last month, the cat may be the victim. A converter does not fix a hole in the manifold flange.

symptom: Cold start rattle for 1–3 seconds, then quiet; sometimes a cam/VTC code
years: 2000s K-series (verify the engine, not the badge)
pattern: Owners have described a cold-start rattle from the VTC actuator for years in public forums and NHTSA complaints. The first cheap look is oil level and viscosity. The expensive look is the actuator. A timing chain is not the automatic first part.
notATsb: Honda issued dealer bulletins on some engines. We will not reproduce them. If a shop cites a bulletin, they can show the OEM number and the oil spec they used.
dummyMove: Record the rattle on your phone at cold start. Ask whether they are quoting an actuator, a chain, or an oil change. One part at a time.
geniusNote: A 0W-20 vs 5W-20 argument is a book spec, not a forum. If the rattle lasts past a few seconds or sets a cam correlation code, that is a different ticket than a 1-second chirp.

symptom: Uses oil, no puddle; misfire on 2AZ-FE four-cylinders
pattern: A widely reported oil-consumption pattern on some 2AZ-FE engines. Public NHTSA investigations and owner complaints exist. The beginner move is a measured consumption test (quarts per 1,000 miles), not a “they all do that.”
notATsb: Toyota had dealer programs and bulletins on some VINs. We will not paste them. SaferCar complaints plus a measured dipstick log are the honest file.
dummyMove: Fill to the stick, write the miles, recheck in 1,000 miles on level ground. Photo the stick. Do not buy a PCV and a hope as a complete diagnosis.
geniusNote: A quart in 1,200 miles is a number. “It always used a little” is not. Low oil plus a misfire is how you buy a cat. Check the stick before the trip.

symptom: A spark plug blew out of a 5.4 3V, or a shop is chasing a misfire on that engine
pattern: The two-piece plug and the aluminum thread are a known public failure. A plug can leave the hole. The repair is threads or an insert, not “just another plug from the aisle.”
notATsb: Ford published service information. We will not reproduce the procedure or torque tables from a paid book. A shop should show you the insert they use and the cylinder they measured.
dummyMove: If a plug is in the fender well, do not drive it. Ask whether they are helicoil / Time-Sert / replace the head — and the price for one hole vs eight.
geniusNote: These plugs can take a special socket. A broken porcelain in the well is a different hour than a clean thread repair. Authorize the inspection of that hole before a set of eight inserts.

symptom: Misfire, P030x, rough idle on coil-on-plug V8s and V6s
pattern: Coil-on-plug boots crack and a single coil dies. The beginner move is swap the coil to another cylinder and see if the misfire digit follows. A full set of eight is a convenience quote, not a diagnosis.
notATsb: Common pattern, not a pirated TSB. If Ford has a coil supersession, the parts counter can show the new SKU. We do not invent stock.
dummyMove: Ask which cylinder and whether they swapped the coil. Translate P030x on /obd.
geniusNote: The last digit of P0303 is the address. Plug, coil, injector, and compression can all live at that address. One test at a time.

symptom: Overheat, mayo on the cap, external coolant leak on a boxer four
pattern: EJ-series head-gasket leaks are a long-running public complaint pattern: external seepage, consumption, or a mix. A pressure test and a combustion-gas test are measurements. A “they all do that” is not.
notATsb: Subaru service information exists. We will not paste gasket part numbers or sealer recipes from a paid portal.
dummyMove: Photo the underside and the cap. Ask for a cooling-system pressure test and whether combustion gas is in the coolant before you authorize heads-off.
geniusNote: Sealer in the bottle is not a gasket. A shop that wants to “try sealer first” on a confirmed combustion leak is selling time. Get the test result in writing.

symptom: Shudder, flare, or “slipping” on a Nissan/Jatco CVT
pattern: Judder and heat-related CVT complaints fill SaferCar for these nameplates. There were public warranty extensions on some VINs. A fluid “flush” on a dying belt is not a guaranteed save.
notATsb: Nissan TSBs and warranty extensions are dealer documents. We will not reproduce them. Run the VIN at the dealer and on SaferCar. Ask for the campaign / extension letter, not a forum PDF.
dummyMove: Record the shudder speed and temperature. Ask whether your VIN is on an extension before you pay a used CVT from a yard.
geniusNote: CVT fluid spec is picky. A generic “universal CVT” pour is how you buy a worse shudder. If they cannot name the Nissan fluid, wait.

symptom: Fuel pump silent, random electrical, no-crank, wipers with a mind of their own (Chrysler/Dodge/Jeep/Ram)
pattern: The Totally Integrated Power Module is a public complaint magnet: fuel-pump relay logic, no-start, and ghost electrics. A fuel pump is the expensive wrong first part when the TIPM never commands it.
notATsb: Chrysler issued recalls and service information on some TIPM populations. Look up the VIN on SaferCar. We will not paste pinouts from a paid wiring book.
dummyMove: Ask whether the pump is being commanded. A cheap test is listen / power at the pump when cranking — before you buy a tank-out pump.
geniusNote: A no-start with a silent pump and a live cluster is a command problem until proven otherwise. Scan and power probe beat a parts cannon.

symptom: Oil on the belt, burning oil smell, leak at the filter housing on a BMW six
pattern: The oil-filter housing gasket and related plastic fittings leak onto the steering belt on several BMW sixes. Public owner photos are everywhere. Oil on a ribbed belt is a roadside no-go, not a “next oil change” leak.
notATsb: BMW has repair instructions. We will not copy labor times or part catalogs from ISTA/ALLDATA.
dummyMove: Photo the belt and the housing. If the belt is wet, ask for a belt plus the gasket — a new gasket on a glazed belt is a comeback.
geniusNote: A $20 gasket can sit behind a belt, a tensioner, and a shop’s minimum. Ask for the photo and whether the belt is in the price. Do not drive it if the belt is shiny with oil.

symptom: Engine dies while rolling, airbags did not deploy, or a 2000s GM compact you are buying used
pattern: GM’s ignition-switch defect is a documented NHTSA case: the switch could move out of run, killing engine and disabling airbags. This is a recall lookup, not a “they fixed those.”
notATsb: Public NHTSA / GM recall. We do not reproduce the switch-comparison photos from the investigation PDFs. Run the VIN.
dummyMove: SaferCar VIN lookup. If the campaign is open, that is a dealer visit — not a used switch from a forum.
geniusNote: A heavy keychain was part of the public story. The fix is the campaign part, not a lecture about keys. Still run the VIN; some cars needed more than one campaign.

symptom: EV will not wake, no climate, “dead” despite a charged traction pack
pattern: The 12-volt (or small support battery) closes contactors and runs computers. A healthy pack plus a dead 12V looks like a brick. Public owner reports are consistent across brands.
notATsb: Owner-manual and field pattern, not a stolen OEM TSB. Each brand’s jump posts differ. Read the book before you clamp.
dummyMove: Ask for a 12V load test and DC-DC output before anyone prices a pack. See /jobs/ev and the EV playbook.
geniusNote: A rested 12.3 V can still fail when contactors pull. The load test is the sentence. Do not crawl orange cables.

symptom: High chirp in the last second of a stop; pedal still firm
pattern: A wear-indicator tab is designed to squeal around 2–3 mm of lining. It is not metal-on-metal. It is not proof the other axle is due. Public “they sold me four corners” complaints start here.
notATsb: A mechanical pattern, not a TSB. No OEM PDF required to ask for millimeters.
dummyMove: Use the brake playbook. Ask for the thinnest pad mm and rotor vs discard. Decline the four-wheel package until they have numbers on the quiet axle.
geniusNote: Aftermarket pads can squeal when they are new — that is glaze or a missing shim, not 2 mm. A new-pad squeal after a job is a comeback, not an MPI.

symptom: Perforated frame, rust flakes on a truck lift, or a used Tundra/Tacoma from the rust belt
pattern: Toyota had public frame-corrosion campaigns on some trucks. A rust-belt used truck can look clean on top and be lace underneath. This is a lift-and-photo job, not a Carfax line.
notATsb: Recall / goodwill campaigns were public. We will not paste Toyota’s inspection criteria. SaferCar plus a lift photo of the rails is the file.
dummyMove: On a PPI, photo the rails, the spare crossmember, and any perforation. Ask whether this VIN was in a frame campaign.
geniusNote: Surface scale is not a hole. A hole you can put a pick through is a structural conversation. Do not buy “we sprayed it” as a close-out.
